Where it began

Laxman Sivaramakrishnan was born in Chennai on 31 December 1965, and was known to almost everyone as Siva. He announced himself early. Playing in a Madras schools championship at the age of 12, he took seven wickets for two runs, a return most bowlers never manage at any level.

At fifteen he toured Sri Lanka with India's Under-19 side, led by Ravi Shastri. A year later he made his first-class debut in a Ranji Trophy quarter-final against Delhi, and his 7 for 28 in their second innings all came inside eleven overs. In the Duleep Trophy soon after, one of his five wickets was Sunil Gavaskar, who offered no stroke to a googly.

The player

With only three first-class matches behind him he was picked for the tours of Pakistan and the West Indies, and he made his Test debut at St John's aged 17 years and 118 days. No Indian had played a Test younger at the time.

His great moment came in his second Test, against England in Bombay. His first Test wicket was Graeme Fowler, caught off his own bowling, and he went on to take 6 for 64 and 6 for 117 as India won by eight wickets, their first Test victory since 1981. At 18 years and 333 days he was the third-youngest bowler to take ten wickets in a Test. Later that season he was the leading wicket-taker at the World Championship of Cricket in Australia, which India won, and he stumped Javed Miandad off a leg break in the final.

He played 9 Tests from 1983 to 1986, taking 26 wickets at 44.04 with three five-wicket innings.

What made him special

He was a wrist-spinner at a time when leg-spin was thought a luxury in one-day cricket, and he proved the doubters wrong by taking wickets and the most catches at that world tournament. India won 12 of the 16 one-day matches he played.

His Test career was brief, and his batting was never the reason anyone bought a ticket: his highest Test score was 25. He answered that in his own way, turning himself into a batsman in domestic cricket and making three hundreds in the 1987/88 season, when Tamil Nadu lifted the Ranji Trophy. He played on for another decade, finishing with Baroda.

Away from the middle

He studied at Ramakrishna Mission Vivekananda College. In 2000 he began a long career as a commentator, starting at Bangladesh's first Test, in Dhaka, and in 2017 he gave his first commentary in Tamil. In May 2013 he joined the ICC's cricket committee as one of the voices of the players.

And finally

His name holds a small puzzle. Sivaramakrishnan is his given name, not his surname; the L stands for his father's given name, Laxmanan, in the Tamil way. Spell out the initial and he appears to share a record for the longest surname in Test cricket, which is quite an achievement for a name that is not a surname at all.
